text:
Mr. Henderson, once feared for his red pen and strict adherence to grammar, now moved with the slow grace of a glacier among the cereal aisles. He clutched a box of 'Cloud Nine' flakes, his knuckles white. Beside him stood Elena, no longer the shy girl who cried over misplaced commas, but a woman in a sharp blazer, scanning items with terrifying efficiency.

"Elena?" he whispered, recognizing the way she tilted her head when calculating discounts.

She turned, eyes widening not with nostalgia, but recognition of a pattern. "Mr. H? You’re still buying the wrong brand."

He blinked. "I... I thought they were on sale."

"They aren't," she said, pulling out her phone. It wasn’t a calculator; it was a live feed of the store’s inventory system. She had become the architect of this very supermarket’s algorithm twenty years ago. Her precision wasn’t just habit; it was code.

"I failed your math test," she recalled softly.

"You did," he agreed. "But you always questioned the logic behind the problems."

She smiled, tapping her screen. The lights in aisle four flickered off, saving three cents per item on every product in sight. "I fixed the lighting grid. You taught me to look for the hidden variables."

They walked together, not as teacher and student, but as two minds that had finally synchronized, leaving a trail of optimized savings in their wake.
